claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe and S. kambucha are 99.5% identical at the DNA sequence level.
source: Sk and Sp are 99.5% identical at the DNA sequence level (Rhind et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhind et al., 2011

claim: Sk/Sp hybrid diploids are mostly infertile.
source: Despite their genetic similarity, Sk/Sp hybrid diploids are mostly infertile (Singh and Klar, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh and Klar, 2002

claim: Sk/Sp hybrid diploids displayed no obvious mitotic defects.
source: Sk/Sp hybrid diploids displayed no obvious mitotic defects, indicating there are no dominant lethal incompatibilities between the two species that act during mitosis (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Sk/Sk diploids had a slightly lower viable spore yield than Sp/Sp diploids, 3.6 vs 8.4.
source: Sk/Sk diploids had a slightly lower viable spore yield than Sp/Sp diploids, 3.6 vs 8.4 (unpaired t test p=0.053; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical test

claim: Spores derived from Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids were equally viable when assayed via micromanipulation of individual spores.
source: However, when assayed via micromanipulation of individual spores, spores derived from Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids were equally viable.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The difference between Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids in the viable spore yield assay is due to an extra mitosis of Sp/Sp diploids before meiotic induction, not higher viability of gametes.
source: We therefore conclude that the difference between Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids in the viable spore yield assay is due to an extra mitosis of Sp/Sp diploids before meiotic induction, not higher viability of gametes.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from micromanipulation data

claim: Sk/Sp hybrids had a viable spore yield at least 24-fold less than that of either of the pure species diploids.
source: In sharp contrast, Sk/Sp hybrids had a viable spore yield at least 24-fold less than that of either of the pure species diploids (t test p<0.01; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical test

claim: Sk/Sp hybrids initiated and completed both meiotic nuclear divisions with similar timing and efficiency compared to Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids.
source: Using DAPI staining of cells, we found that Sk/Sp hybrids initiated and completed both meiotic nuclear divisions with similar timing and efficiency compared to Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk diploids (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Spore inviability in products of hybrid meiosis is not due to an inability to enter meiosis or due to checkpoint activation preventing the completion of the meiotic divisions.
source: These results suggest that spore inviability in products of hybrid meiosis is not due to an inability to enter meiosis or due to checkpoint activation preventing the completion of the meiotic divisions.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from meiotic progression data

claim: The spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids were more irregular and less refractile than those produced by pure species diploids.
source: However, we did find that the spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids were more irregular and less refractile than those produced by pure species diploids (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by visual observation shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: The viable spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids grew into colonies that were grossly different from those of pure species controls.
source: Furthermore, the viable spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids grew into colonies that were grossly different from those of pure species controls (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by visual observation shown in Figure 1G

claim: Most viable spore colonies from Sk/Sp hybrids were small and many had irregularly shaped edges, rather than large colonies with smooth circular perimeters like those produced by pure species spores.
source: There were a few large colonies from the hybrid spores, but most were small and many had irregularly shaped edges, rather than large colonies with smooth circular perimeters like those produced by pure species spores.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: When the small hybrid spore colonies were streaked for single colonies on fresh Petri plates, some cells within the colony lost the slow growth phenotype and generated colonies similar in size to those of Sp or Sk haploids.
source: When the small hybrid spore colonies were streaked for single colonies on fresh Petri plates, some cells within the colony lost the slow growth phenotype and generated colonies similar in size to those of Sp or Sk haploids.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The small colonies from hybrid spores are consistent with being chromosome 3 aneuploids (disomes).
source: These phenotypes are consistent with the small colonies being chromosome 3 aneuploids (disomes); aneuploidy for chromosome 1 or 2 is lethal in Sp (Niwa et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on phenotype and citation to Niwa et al., 2006

claim: Aneuploidy for chromosome 1 or 2 is lethal in Sp.
source: These phenotypes are consistent with the small colonies being chromosome 3 aneuploids (disomes); aneuploidy for chromosome 1 or 2 is lethal in Sp (Niwa et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2006

claim: From Sk/Sp hybrids, 33% of the viable spores were heterozygous aneuploids and 44% were heterozygous diploid, significantly more than the 2.2 and 3.5%, respectively, observed in Sk control diploids.
source: From Sk/Sp hybrids, 33% of the viable spores were heterozygous aneuploids and 44% were heterozygous diploid, significantly more than the 2.2 and 3.5%, respectively, observed in Sk control diploids (Figure 1H; p<0.01 for both; G-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H with statistical test

claim: In many eukaryotes, meiotic recombination is essential for the production of viable gametes.
source: In many eukaryotes, meiotic recombination is essential for the production of viable gametes.
evidence: General scientific knowledge

claim: Recombination can form crossovers, which help ensure proper disjunction of homologous chromosome pairs during the first meiotic division.
source: This is because recombination can form crossovers, which help ensure proper disjunction of homologous chromosome pairs during the first meiotic division (Kerr et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerr et al., 2012

claim: In both budding yeast and mouse hybrids, defects in meiotic recombination are major causes of hybrid infertility.
source: In both budding yeast and mouse hybrids, defects in meiotic recombination are major causes of hybrid infertility (Hunter et al., 1996; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Mihola et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunter et al., 1996; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Mihola et al., 2009

claim: Rapid evolution of genes that function in meiotic recombination has led to the hypothesis that recombination defects serve as a general barrier to genetic exchange between species.
source: These observations, combined with rapid evolution of genes that function in meiotic recombination, have led to the hypothesis that recombination defects serve as a general barrier to genetic exchange between species (Rhind et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2009; Sawyer and Malik, 2006; Myers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rhind et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2009; Sawyer and Malik, 2006; Myers et al., 2010

claim: Meiotic recombination is initiated by double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) induced by a complex of proteins including the conserved Spo11 protein (Rec12 in fission yeast).
source: Meiotic recombination is initiated by double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) induced by a complex of proteins including the conserved Spo11 protein (Rec12 in fission yeast).
evidence: General scientific knowledge

claim: In many organisms, including Sp, meiotic DSBs are not randomly distributed; rather they are concentrated in regions called hotspots.
source: In many organisms, including Sp, meiotic DSBs are not randomly distributed; rather they are concentrated in regions called hotspots (Cromie et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cromie et al., 2007

claim: DSB hotspots are thought to evolve rapidly because they can be lost due to biased gene conversion during break repair.
source: DSB hotspots are thought to evolve rapidly because they can be lost due to biased gene conversion during break repair (Boulton et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boulton et al., 1997

claim: Rapid divergence of a DSB hotspot-determining protein contributes to infertility of certain mouse hybrids and some human males.
source: Perhaps related to this, rapid divergence of a DSB hotspot-determining protein contributes to infertility of certain mouse hybrids and some human males (Mihola et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010; Segurel et al., 2011; Baudat et al., 2010; Irie et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mihola et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010; Segurel et al., 2011; Baudat et al., 2010; Irie et al., 2009

claim: The overall genome-wide pattern of DSB hotspots in Sk was similar to the published Sp hotspot map.
source: Qualitatively, we found that the overall genome-wide pattern of DSB hotspots in Sk was similar to the published Sp hotspot map (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Cromie et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Cromie et al., 2007

claim: There is strong correlation between hotspot intensities in Sk and Sp at 286 previously identified Sp hotspots.
source: We then compared the DSB hotspots between Sk and Sp at 286 previously identified Sp hotspots and found strong correlation between hotspot intensities in the two species (Figure 2A; Fowler et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Fowler et al., 2013

claim: Hotspots have largely not diverged between Sp and Sk, so such divergence is unlikely to contribute to hybrid infertility.
source: This result shows that hotspots have largely not diverged between Sp and Sk, so such divergence is unlikely to contribute to hybrid infertility.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from hotspot correlation data

claim: Sk/Sp cells are proficient at inducing DSBs.
source: Sk/Sp cells are proficient at inducing DSBs. Ethidium bromide stained pulsed-field gel of diploids at 0 and 8.5 hr after inducing meiosis in liquid cultures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: DSBs are formed at similar locations and similar frequencies in Sk/Sp and Sk/Sk.
source: We find that DSBs are formed at similar locations and similar frequencies in Sk/Sp and Sk/Sk.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: DSBs are efficiently repaired in Sk/Sp.
source: DSBs are efficiently repaired in Sk/Sp. Ethidium bromide stained pulsed-field gel of rad50+ diploids at the given times after the induction of meiosis show that DSBs do not accumulate more in Sk/Sp than the Sp/Sp control during meiotic prophase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Sk/Sp hybrids form and efficiently repair DSBs.
source: Together with those in (B) these data demonstrate that Sk/Sp cells form and efficiently repair DSBs.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from DSB formation and repair data

claim: Both Sk and hybrid diploids exhibited similar amounts of breakage at the same sites at known meiotic DSB hotspots.
source: For a more precise view of DSB formation in hybrids, we assayed break formation in rad50S diploids at known meiotic DSB hotspots contained on the NotI restriction fragments designated 'J' (0.5 Mb) and 'D' (1.1 Mb) of the Sp genome (Cromie et al., 2007). We found that both Sk and hybrid diploids exhibited similar amounts of breakage at the same sites, in accord with the microarray results above (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D and citation to Cromie et al., 2007

claim: Chromosomes of Sk/Sp diploids were largely intact throughout meiotic prophase.
source: To assay DSB repair, we visualized meiotic chromosomes via PFGE in rad50+ (DSB repair proficient) diploids. As in pure species, chromosomes of Sk/Sp diploids were largely intact throughout meiotic prophase (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The breaks that form in Sk/Sp hybrids are efficiently repaired.
source: This shows that the breaks that form (e.g., Figure 2B) are efficiently repaired.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from DSB repair data

claim: DSB formation is grossly normal in Sk/Sp hybrids and the breaks are repaired efficiently.
source: Together, these results suggest that DSB formation is grossly normal in Sk/Sp hybrids and that the breaks are repaired efficiently.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from DSB formation and repair data

claim: Meiotic recombination promotes fertility but is not essential for producing viable spores in Sp.
source: Meiotic recombination promotes fertility but is not essential for producing viable spores in Sp (Davis and Smith, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davis and Smith, 2003

claim: Random segregation of three chromosome pairs at the first meiotic division would frequently (∼25% of the time) result in a viable chromosome complement: haploid, diploid, or chromosome 3 disome.
source: This is largely because random segregation of three chromosome pairs at the first meiotic division would frequently (∼25% of the time) result in a viable chromosome complement: haploid, diploid, or chromosome 3 disome.
evidence: Inference based on probability calculation

claim: Sp has a recombination-independent chromosome segregation system that is partially effective in promoting proper chromosome segregation.
source: In addition, Sp, like some other species, has a recombination-independent chromosome segregation system that is partially effective in promoting proper chromosome segregation (Davis and Smith, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davis and Smith, 2003

claim: Both Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk rec12Δ mutant diploids had viable spore yields fourfold to fivefold lower than the corresponding rec12+ diploids.
source: As expected, when we eliminated nearly all meiotic recombination by deleting rec12 (rec12Δ), both Sp/Sp and Sk/Sk rec12Δ mutant diploids had viable spore yields fourfold to fivefold lower than the corresponding rec12+ diploids (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: A similar decrease in fertility was not observed in rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrid diploids: their viable spore yield was indistinguishable from that of rec12+ hybrid diploids.
source: Surprisingly, a similar decrease in fertility was not observed in rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrid diploids: their viable spore yield was indistinguishable from that of rec12+ hybrid diploids (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Recombination does not promote Sk/Sp hybrid fertility, unlike in pure species.
source: This result demonstrates that recombination does not promote Sk/Sp hybrid fertility, unlike in pure species.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from rec12Δ fertility data

claim: Sk/Sp hybrids fail to form crossovers and/or the recombination events that occur in hybrids hurt fertility just as much as they promote it.
source: This could be because Sk/Sp hybrids fail to form crossovers and/or because the recombination events that occur in hybrids hurt fertility just as much as they promote it.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: Recombination frequencies in Sk/Sk were lower than those in Sp/Sp in at least two genetic intervals.
source: We found that recombination frequencies in Sk/Sk were lower than those in Sp/Sp in at least two genetic intervals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Young et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Young et al., 2002

claim: More dramatic decreases in observed recombinant frequencies were observed in several genetic intervals amongst viable spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids compared to Sp/Sp.
source: We also observed more dramatic decreases in observed recombinant frequencies in several genetic intervals amongst viable spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids compared to Sp/Sp (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3

claim: The magnitude of the decrease in recombinant frequencies was greatest in the lys1-lys7 interval where there was >40-fold decrease in genetic distance in hybrids compared to Sp/Sp.
source: The magnitude of the decrease was greatest in the lys1-lys7 interval where we observed >40-fold decrease in genetic distance in hybrids compared to Sp/Sp.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Large decreases in recombination could be explained if some DSBs are infrequently repaired as crossovers in hybrids, or if the crossovers they produce generate inviable chromosomes, for instance due to chromosomal rearrangements.
source: Large decreases in recombination could be explained if some DSBs are infrequently repaired as crossovers in hybrids, or if the crossovers they produce generate inviable chromosomes, for instance due to chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: A large region of chromosome 1 (between base pairs 2,683,632 and 4,911,515) is inverted in the Sp genome, relative to Sk.
source: To address this latter possibility, we resequenced the Sk genome ('Materials and methods') (Rhind et al., 2011), which revealed that a large region of chromosome 1 (between base pairs 2,683,632 and 4,911,515) is inverted in the Sp genome, relative to Sk (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing data and citation to Rhind et al., 2011

claim: The chromosome 1 inversion has been previously described.
source: This inversion has been previously described (Brown et al., 2011; Teresa Avelar et al., 2013) and it occurred in the Sp lineage (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011; Teresa Avelar et al., 2013

claim: The chromosome 1 inversion occurred in the Sp lineage.
source: This inversion has been previously described (Brown et al., 2011; Teresa Avelar et al., 2013) and it occurred in the Sp lineage (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011

claim: Odd numbers of crossovers within the chromosome 1 inversion would cause lethal chromosomal rearrangements (duplications of one arm and deletion of the other).
source: Odd numbers of crossovers within this inversion would cause lethal chromosomal rearrangements (duplications of one arm and deletion of the other).
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: Odd numbers of crossovers within the chromosome 1 inversion would cause spore inviability and likely explains why rec12+ Sk/Sp hybrids do not have higher fertility than rec12Δ hybrids.
source: This would cause spore inviability and likely explains why rec12+ Sk/Sp hybrids do not have higher fertility than rec12Δ hybrids, since odd numbers of crossovers within the inversion would likely impair viable spore recovery as much as an absence of recombination (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge and data shown in Figure 3

claim: The recombination pattern of markers across chromosome 1 is consistent with the interpretation that the inversion explains reduced recombinant frequencies.
source: The recombination pattern of markers across chromosome 1 is consistent with this interpretation.
evidence: Inference based on recombination data

claim: The lys1-lys7 interval, in which the greatest reduction in recombinants was observed, is located within the inversion.
source: The lys1-lys7 interval, in which we observed the greatest reduction in recombinants, is located within the inversion (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3

claim: The next highest reduction in recombinant frequencies was between markers flanking the inversion boundary.
source: The next highest reduction in recombinant frequencies was between markers flanking the inversion boundary (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3

claim: Recombination frequencies outside the inversion were only ∼twofold to eightfold decreased in hybrids compared Sp/Sp diploids.
source: In contrast, recombination frequencies outside the inversion were only ∼twofold to eightfold decreased in hybrids compared Sp/Sp diploids (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3

claim: The non-inversion associated differences in recombination frequencies are not a hybrid-specific defect and may be due to different recombination frequencies in Sk and Sp, perhaps caused by different DSB frequencies or different DSB repair outcomes.
source: These non-inversion associated differences are not a hybrid-specific defect and may be due to different recombination frequencies in Sk and Sp, perhaps caused by different DSB frequencies or different DSB repair outcomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference based on recombination data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a surprising genetic linkage between leu1 and ade6 in Sk/Sp hybrids, despite the fact that these genes are located on chromosomes 2 and 3, respectively, in both species.
source: Our analyses of recombination also revealed a surprising genetic linkage between leu1 and ade6 in Sk/Sp hybrids, despite the fact that these genes are located on chromosomes 2 and 3, respectively, in both species (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: There is a reciprocal translocation between Sk chromosomes 2 and 3, relative to Sp.
source: We speculated that there was a reciprocal translocation between Sk chromosomes 2 and 3, relative to Sp.
evidence: Speculation based on genetic linkage data

claim: If the translocation included essential genes, it would render gametes with non-parental chromosome combinations of the affected arms inviable; this inviability would also create the semblance of genetic linkage between the two chromosomes.
source: If such a translocation included essential genes, it would render gametes with non-parental chromosome combinations of the affected arms inviable; this inviability would also create the semblance of genetic linkage between the two chromosomes.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: Essential genes (alr2 and SPCP1E11.08) had swapped chromosome locations between Sk and Sp.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found using Southern blot analyses that essential genes (alr2 and SPCP1E11.08) had swapped chromosome locations between Sk and Sp (Figure 4B,C; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4B,C and citation to Kim et al., 2010

claim: The translocation junctions were mapped to position 676,281 on Sp chromosome 2 and 1,932,034 on Sp chromosome 3.
source: We partially assembled the Sk genome to map the translocation junctions to position 676,281 on Sp chromosome 2 and 1,932,034 on Sp chromosome 3.
evidence: Supported by genome assembly data

claim: The translocation junctions were verified via PCR.
source: We verified the translocation junctions via PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5

claim: Analyses of synteny in two outgroup species (S. octosporus and S. cryophilus) showed that the translocation occurred in the Sk lineage.
source: Analyses of synteny in two outgroup species (S. octosporus and S. cryophilus; Rhind et al., 2011) showed that the translocation occurred in the Sk lineage.
evidence: Supported by synteny analysis and citation to Rhind et al., 2011

claim: The translocation appears to have resulted from a crossover between a Tf transposon found in Sk on chromosome 2 (corresponding to a single Tf transposon LTR in Sp) and a Tf transposon unique to Sk on chromosome 3.
source: The translocation appears to have resulted from a crossover between a Tf transposon found in Sk on chromosome 2 (corresponding to a single Tf transposon LTR in Sp) and a Tf transposon unique to Sk on chromosome 3.
evidence: Inference based on sequence analysis

claim: Chromosomal rearrangements are likely a significant contributor to Sp/Sk hybrid infertility.
source: Thus, we find that chromosomal rearrangements are likely a significant contributor to Sp/Sk hybrid infertility.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from rearrangement data

claim: Recombination defects due to chromosome rearrangements are not sufficient to explain the near complete hybrid sterility in Sk/Sp hybrids.
source: However, our findings suggested that recombination defects due to chromosome rearrangements are not sufficient to explain the near complete hybrid sterility we see in Sk/Sp hybrids for several reasons.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrid diploids still have greater than six-fold lower viable spore yield than rec12Δ Sk/Sk or Sp/Sp (pure species) diploids.
source: First, rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrid diploids still have greater than six-fold lower viable spore yield than rec12Δ Sk/Sk or Sp/Sp (pure species) diploids (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The chromosome 2-chromosome 3 reciprocal translocation predicts only a two-fold lower viable spore yield because only half of the gametes would inherit an incompatible chromosome combination.
source: The chromosome 2-chromosome 3 reciprocal translocation predicts only a two-fold lower viable spore yield because only half of the gametes would inherit an incompatible chromosome combination.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: If defects in recombination cause errors in chromosome segregation leading to the production of aneuploid and diploid gametes, the frequency of aneuploid and diploid spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids in the absence of meiotic recombination (rec12Δ) should be similar to the frequencies observed in rec12Δ pure species controls.
source: Second, if defects in recombination cause errors in chromosome segregation leading to the production of aneuploid and diploid gametes (e.g., Davis and Smith, 2003), we would expect that the frequency of aneuploid and diploid spores produced by Sk/Sp hybrids in the absence of meiotic recombination (rec12Δ) should be similar to the frequencies observed in rec12Δ pure species controls.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge and citation to Davis and Smith, 2003

claim: The level of heterozygous aneuploids and diploids in rec12Δ hybrids is still significantly (at least twofold) higher than that observed in both rec12Δ Sk/Sk and rec12Δ Sp/Sp controls.
source: In contrast to this expectation, we find that the level of heterozygous aneuploids and diploids in rec12Δ hybrids is still significantly (at least twofold) higher than that observed in both rec12Δ Sk/Sk and rec12Δ Sp/Sp controls (Figure 5A,B; p<0.01 for both; G-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B with statistical test

claim: Something other than recombination defects contributes to the high fraction of diploids and aneuploids, as well as the low viable spore yield.
source: This result indicates that something other than recombination defects contributes to the high fraction of diploids and aneuploids, as well as the low viable spore yield.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from aneuploidy data

claim: There were very small differences in the proportion of aneuploids that were generated in hybrids vs pure species meiosis.
source: Our analyses revealed very small differences in the proportion of aneuploids that were generated in hybrids vs pure species meiosis (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The higher recovery of aneuploid and diploid spores from Sk/Sp hybrids is a result of lower viability of haploid spores.
source: We therefore conclude that the higher recovery of aneuploid and diploid spores from Sk/Sp hybrids is a result of lower viability of haploid spores.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from aneuploidy frequency data

claim: The lower viability of haploid spores could be partially explained by the incompatibility between Sp and Sk chromosomes 2 and 3 due to the reciprocal translocation in Sk.
source: The lower viability of haploid spores could be partially explained by the incompatibility between Sp and Sk chromosomes 2 and 3 due to the reciprocal translocation in Sk.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: Aneuploids with Sk and Sp chromosome 3 (chromosome 3 disomes) will contain all essential genes, whereas haploids must inherit chromosomes 2 and 3 from the same species to be viable.
source: Aneuploids with Sk and Sp chromosome 3 (chromosome 3 disomes) will contain all essential genes, whereas haploids must inherit chromosomes 2 and 3 from the same species to be viable.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: The translocation scenario predicts only a twofold advantage of aneuploidy, yet rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrids produce at least threefold more aneuploids than pure species rec12Δ controls.
source: This scenario, however, predicts only a twofold advantage of aneuploidy, yet rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrids produce at least threefold more aneuploids than pure species rec12Δ controls.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of expected and observed data

claim: Eliminating the chr2-chr3 incompatibility did not mitigate the aneuploidy phenotype.
source: Furthermore, eliminating the chr2-chr3 incompatibility (see below) did not mitigate the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The viability benefit conferred by aneuploidy is due to disomy or heterozygosity for an allele(s) on chromosome 3.
source: We therefore hypothesize that the viability benefit conferred by aneuploidy is due to disomy or heterozygosity for an allele(s) on chromosome 3.
evidence: Hypothesis based on inference from data

claim: The viability benefit of aneuploidy could be due to a protective effect exerted by the Sk chromosome 3 within gametes containing Sp chromosome 3 and vice versa.
source: This could, for example, be due to a protective effect exerted by the Sk chromosome 3 within gametes containing Sp chromosome 3 and vice versa ('Discussion').
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: In all cases, the Sk allele was transmitted to more viable spores than the Sp allele.
source: Surprisingly, we found that in all cases, the Sk allele was transmitted to more viable spores than the Sp allele (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The overrepresentation of Sk alleles was not specific to the markers used, or which species contributed the marked (mutant) allele to the Sk/Sp hybrid diploid.
source: This phenotype was not specific to the markers used, or which species contributed the marked (mutant) allele to the Sk/Sp hybrid diploid.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The overrepresentation of Sk alleles from chromosomes 1 and 2 in the viable spores was observed within both haploid and aneuploid spores.
source: In addition, the overrepresentation of Sk alleles from chromosomes 1 and 2 in the viable spores was observed within both haploid and aneuploid spores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The enhanced transmission of Sk alleles on chromosomes 1 and 2 is independent of the aneuploidy phenotype.
source: This suggests the enhanced transmission of Sk alleles on these chromosomes is independent of the aneuploidy phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on data showing drive in both haploid and aneuploid spores

claim: Genetic markers nearer to any driving locus would be expected to show a stronger transmission bias than those that are more distantly linked.
source: Genetic markers nearer to any driving locus would be expected to show a stronger transmission bias than those that are more distantly linked.
evidence: General genetic knowledge

claim: On chromosome 1, the driving locus is closer to lys1 than to ura1 or arg3.
source: On chromosome 1, the transmission bias of Sk lys1 (72%) was stronger than those of both ura1 (55%) and arg3 (58%), indicating that the driving locus is closer to lys1 than to ura1 or arg3.
evidence: Inference based on transmission bias data

claim: On chromosome 2, the driving locus is closer to leu1 than to his5, his4, lys4, or ade8.
source: On chromosome 2, the driving locus is closer to leu1 (94% Sk transmission bias) than to his5 (67%), his4, lys4, or ade8 (all ∼64%).
evidence: Inference based on transmission bias data

claim: The driving locus on chromosome 3 is closer to ade6 than to ura4.
source: The driving locus on chromosome 3 is closer to ade6 (82%) than to ura4 (52%).
evidence: Inference based on transmission bias data

claim: The significant overrepresentation of Sk alleles on all three chromosomes was also observed in spores produced by rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrids.
source: The significant overrepresentation of Sk alleles on all three chromosomes was also observed in spores produced by rec12Δ Sk/Sp hybrids (p<0.01 G-test; Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical test

claim: The transmission of alleles was altered by the absence of recombination.
source: However, the transmission of alleles was altered by the absence of recombination.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The alteration in allele transmission in the absence of recombination was expected due to stronger linkage with the driving locus in the absence of recombination.
source: This was expected due to stronger linkage with the driving locus in the absence of recombination.
evidence: Inference based on genetic knowledge

claim: his5 is distantly linked to the chromosome 2 driving locus in rec12+ but appears more closely linked to it in the absence of recombination in rec12Δ.
source: For example, his5 is distantly linked to the chromosome 2 driving locus in rec12+ but appears more closely linked to it in the absence of recombination in rec12Δ (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: If Sp gene A was incompatible with Sk gene B, but Sk gene A was compatible with both Sp and Sk alleles of gene B, Sk gene A would be over-represented in the surviving gametes.
